steps.message:
This is a reverse-engineering task. You are given a compiled program and its documentation. Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided program and reading its documentation.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this task.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary, or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. Your submission must not embed a copy of the provided executable, and your program must work without it.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code
The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries (`cargo install <project>`, `go get <module>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, ...)
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary
Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for observation only — your final solution must not depend on it, or on any other pre-built version of the same tool, at runtime or at build time.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary
- Copying, encoding (base64, hex, compression, archives) or embedding the provided binary in your submission
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable or copies it
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external copy of the tool

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable
All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it through its normal user interface (command-line arguments, stdin/stdout/stderr, files, environment variables).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

This restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You may use any analysis tools on binaries that you build yourself.

## What IS allowed
- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, arguments, files and environment variables to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Task context

The workspace is `/workspace` (a git repository). It contains:
- `./executable` — the program to reproduce (you can run it, but not read it).
- Its user documentation: `LICENSE`, `README.md`, `docs/assets/social-preview.html`.

## Your task

Implement the source code for a program with exactly the same behavior as `./executable`: the same output on stdout and stderr, the same exit codes, and the same effects on files.
- Write your implementation in Go, the language of the original program (Go 1.27.3, standard library only). `./compile.sh` must build it from your source code into a native executable. Do not write it in another language or have your program run another language's interpreter (Python, Perl, Node.js, ...), and write at least 50 lines of Go source. All code in your workspace counts, not only your program: code in other languages (shell, Python, Perl, ...), including your own test scripts and tools, must stay at most 5% of the workspace's code lines. Keep scratch scripts outside the workspace (for example in /tmp), or write your tests in Go.
- No project-specific dependencies are pre-installed and you do NOT have access to the internet, so you cannot download packages. Use only the standard libraries and tools already installed.
- Provide an executable `./compile.sh` at the workspace root that builds your program and leaves the final compiled Go binary (a native executable, not a script or launcher) at `./executable` in the workspace root. `./compile.sh` must succeed on a fresh checkout of your repository without internet access.
- `./compile.sh` must not depend on `./executable` or a `./target` build directory already being present.
- Make sure the executable and every build artifact are listed in `.gitignore`, then commit your work.

You SHOULD extensively test the executable to understand its behavior before and while writing code. Match the original's behavior in full, not only on the inputs you happen to try. If the program has an interactive terminal interface, `tmux` is installed to help you drive it.

## Recommended workflow
1. Read all documentation files.
2. Explore the executable's behavior systematically: `--help`, every subcommand and flag, normal inputs, edge cases, and error cases.
3. Design and write your implementation, then compare its behavior with the original on many inputs.
4. Run `./compile.sh` from a clean checkout to make sure it works, and commit.

When you are completely done, commit your work and stop.
I'll start by exploring the workspace and reading the documentation.

declscope

[![CI](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/mpyw/declscope/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/mpyw/declscope) [![Go Reference](https://pkg.go.dev/badge/github.com/mpyw/declscope.svg)](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/mpyw/declscope)

Write-ups: 🇯🇵 JP · 🇺🇸 EN

Keep your Go packages **flat** without letting them turn into a free-for-all. declscope holds each declaration to the file that declares it. Another file may not use it. This is the `private` that Go has no word for, checked at build time. ## Why Go has two levels of visibility, and the lower one covers the whole package. | Level | Reach | | --- | --- | | Exported | Every importer | | Unexported | **Every file in the package** | There is no third level. In a flat package, every helper is a package-wide name, and every field is a package-wide reach. Splitting the package to get a boundary has a price. - Import cycles, and interfaces written only to break them. - **Every name the two halves share has to be exported.** You wanted a boundary between two files, and you published an API. - **A wrong boundary costs more.** Moving a declaration between files is free. Moving it between packages breaks every importer. `internal/` does not help here. It limits who may import a package, but it adds no level below unexported. So most Go code is better off flat, and the cost appears inside the package. Teams handle this with a convention: *this helper belongs to this file.* The convention lives only in the heads of the people who wrote the package. An AI agent does not know it either. It sees an unexported helper in scope, so it calls it. It sees an unexported field, so it writes to it. Each edit compiles and passes a quick review, and the package becomes a mesh. declscope checks the convention instead. When an agent crosses a boundary, it is told what it crossed and given a fix. The decision is then written in the source, where the next agent reads it. ### What it reports One `database` package holds a repository per entity. ```go // user_repository.go package database import ( "context" "database/sql" "strings" "example.com/app/domain" ) type UserRepository struct{ db *sql.DB } func (r *UserRepository) Find(ctx context.Context, id int64) (*domain.User, error) { row := r.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = ?`, id) return scanUser(row) } func scanUser(row *sql.Row) (*domain.User, error) { var u domain.User var email string if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &email); err != nil { return nil, err } u.Email = normalizeEmail(email) return &u, nil } func normalizeEmail(s string) string { return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s)) } ``` ```go // order_repository.go package database import ( "database/sql" "example.com/app/domain" ) type OrderRepository struct{ db *sql.DB } func scanOrder(rows *sql.Rows) (domain.Order, error) { var o domain.Order var email string if err := rows.Scan(&o.ID, &email); err != nil { return domain.Order{}, err } o.BuyerEmail = normalizeEmail(email) return o, nil } ``` The two scan helpers are named apart by hand, since only one could be called `scan`. That mark says which repository owns which helper, and nothing holds anyone to it. `normalizeEmail` was written for `scanUser`. `scanOrder` calls it, and the compiler accepts that. ```console $ declscope ./... user_repository.go:28:6: func normalizeEmail is private to namespace "userRepository", but is used from namespace "orderRepository" order_repository.go:17:17: used here, in namespace "orderRepository" ``` A crossing has two answers. | Answer | How | | --- | --- | | Keep the boundary | Move the call inside the namespace | | Share on purpose | Write `//declscope:shared`, which `-fix` inserts | Here the helper belongs to neither repository. The repair is a third file, and a stated scope. ```go // email.go package database import "strings" //declscope:shared func normalizeEmail(s string) string { return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s)) } ``` > [!TIP] > `-fix` always widens, because that is the repair a tool can apply. It writes the directive where the declaration stands, and never moves a declaration to another file. Where the boundary is worth keeping, move the call yourself. ### Where declscope sits Three linters draw boundaries in Go, at three scales. ![A Go program drawn as nested frames. Between the api and database packages, depguard asks whether one package may import another. A green arrow runs from api to database, and a red one back from database to api is crossed out. Inside database, between user_repository.go and order_repository.go, declscope asks whether one file may reach another's declaration. A red arrow from scanOrder to normalizeEmail is crossed out. At the edge of the program, deadcode asks whether anything is reachable at all. The mail package sits greyed out with no arrow entering it, captioned unreachable.](docs/boundaries.png) | Linter | Scale | The question it answers | | --- | --- | --- | | [`depguard`](https://github.com/OpenPeeDeeP/depguard) | Between packages | May this package import that one? | | **declscope** | Within one package | May this file reach that declaration? | | [`deadcode`](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode) | Whole program | Is this reachable at all? | The three compose. `depguard` keeps the package graph honest, declscope keeps each package honest inside, and `deadcode` removes what neither needs to reach. ## Install | Method | Command | Needs | | --- | --- | --- | | **[mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/)** *(recommended)* | `mise use "github:mpyw/declscope@0.24.1"` | Nothing. Installs the prebuilt binary | | `go tool` | `go get -tool github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest` | Go 1.27+ | | `go install` | `go install github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest` | Go 1.27+ | | Release archive | See below | Nothing | ```bash declscope ./... ```
Pin a version, run through go vet, or install from an archive `mise use` pins the version in the project's `mise.toml`, so every checkout and CI run the same one. Add `-g` to install it for every project on your machine instead. ```toml [tools] "github:mpyw/declscope" = "0.24.1" ``` As a tool dependency in `go.mod`: ```bash go get -tool github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest go tool declscope ./... ``` Through `go vet`, which runs it with the same package loading as the rest of your vet checks: ```bash go vet -vettool=$(which declscope) ./... ``` > [!WARNING] > **`go vet` does not see changes to config or baseline files.** It caches the result of each package, and the cache key does not include these files. After a change to either one, run `go vet` once with **`-a`**: > > ```bash > go vet -a -vettool=$(which declscope) ./... > ``` > > Without `-a`, `go vet` can report the result of the old configuration. New diagnostics can be missing, and old ones can remain. Running `declscope` directly is not affected. Without installing anything: ```bash go run github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest ./... ``` From a release archive, verified against the published checksums: ```bash VERSION=0.24.1 curl -LO "https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/releases/download/v${VERSION}/declscope_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz" curl -LO "https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt" shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing tar xzf "declscope_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz" ```
### Flags | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-config` | *(discovered)* | Path to a YAML config file. Skips the [`.declscope.yaml` lookup](#configuration) | | `-test` | `true` | Analyze `*_test.go` files as well | | `-fix` | `false` | Apply suggested fixes | | `-diff` | `false` | With `-fix`, print a diff instead of writing files | | `-V=full` | | Print the version and exit. `go run`, or a build with `-buildvcs=false`, answers `devel` | `-test`, `-fix` and `-diff` come from `go/analysis`. `declscope -help` lists the rest. ### Subcommands | Command | What it does | Flags of its own | | --- | --- | --- | | `declscope survey [packages]` | [Report what was checked and what it found](#measuring-what-is-there), one row per package | `-format`, `-test`, `-config`, `-allow-errors` | | `declscope inspect ` | [Report the shape of one package](#measuring-what-is-there): its namespaces and the crossings between them | `-format`, `-test`, `-config` | | `declscope baseline [packages]` | [Record the violations a codebase already has](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase), `shrink`'s included | `-config`, `-o`, `-shrink`, `-merge` | | `declscope shrink [packages]` | [Unexport what no importer uses](#unexporting-what-no-importer-uses), inside `internal/` | `-fix`, `-config` | | `declscope skill install` | Install the authoring and adoption skills for an AI agent | `--agent`, `--scope` | `declscope -help` lists each one's flags. ## Configuration Every setting is optional. The table below lists each setting and its default value. The YAML block shows all available keys; some values are examples. ```yaml defaults: unexported: private # shared | private rules: naming: qualify: never # always | never | ondemand exported: false # true | false vocabulary: mouse: [wheel] boundary: on # off | on surplus: strict # off | loose | strict unused: strict # off | loose | strict filter: only: [] # nothing outside these, when set omit: - "**/mock_*.go" # and not these baseline: .declscope-baseline.yaml ``` | Key | Values | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `defaults.unexported` | `shared`, `private` | `private` | Scope of a declaration that carries no directive and inherits none | | `rules.naming.qualify` | `always`, `never`, `ondemand` | `never` | When a name must carry its namespace. See [the naming rule](#when-it-applies) | | `rules.naming.exported` | `true`, `false` | `false` | Whether the naming rule also reaches exported declarations. The rename is never offered there | | `rules.naming.vocabulary` | Namespace to a list of words | None | Extra words that carry a namespace. See [what carries a namespace](#what-carries-a-namespace) | | `rules.boundary` | `off`, `on` | `on` | Whether the [`boundary`](#boundary) rule reports. See [reach without a boundary](#reach-without-a-boundary) | | `rules.surplus` | `off`, `loose`, `strict` | `strict` | How much the [`surplus`](#surplus) rule reports. See [strict](#strict) | | `rules.unused` | `off`, `loose`, `strict` | `strict` | How much the [`unused`](#unused-directives) rule reports. See [off, loose and strict](#off-loose-and-strict) | | `filter.only` | Path globs | None | When set, no file outside them is read. Empty places no restriction | | `filter.omit` | Path globs | None | Files taken back out, whether or not `only` let them through | | `baseline` | A path relative to the config file | The nearest `.declscope-baseline.yaml` | The [baseline](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase) to consult | > [!TIP] > For the recommended checks, put this in `.declscope.yaml`: > > ```yaml > rules: > naming: > qualify: ondemand > exported: true > ``` > > `ondemand` checks names once a package has a second namespace. `exported: true` includes exported declarations. `surplus` and `unused` default to `strict`. - The file is `.declscope.yaml` or `.declscope.yml`. An empty one changes nothing. - [`-config`](#flags) names one file, and reads no other. - An **unknown key is an error**, and so is a value a key does not accept. The message names what the section does take, so a typo never leaves a rule at its default in silence. `defaults` takes only `unexported`, because an exported declaration has no scope to default. ### How two config files compose Every `.declscope.yaml` between the analyzed package and the module root is read, **outermost first**. A nearer file does not replace the one above it. Each key composes on its own. | Key | Down the chain | | --- | --- | | `defaults.*`, `rules.*` except `vocabulary`, `baseline` | The nearest file that states the key wins. A key no file states takes the built-in default | | `rules.naming.vocabulary` | Merged per namespace. The nearer file wins the namespaces it states | | `filter.only` | **Intersected.** A file is read when it matches every stating file's list | | `filter.omit` | **Unioned.** A file matching any level's list is not read | > [!IMPORTANT] > **A config file can only ever shrink what is read.** An `omit` written at the root holds everywhere below it, and no nested file can undo it. `filter` has no negation, so nothing like `.gitignore`'s `!` can put a path back. ### The filter rule `filter` decides which files are read at all. A file matches a list when it matches **any** pattern in it. | Written | Read | | --- | --- | | Neither | Every file | | `only` alone | Nothing outside the patterns | | `omit` alone | Everything except the patterns | | Both | What `only` admits, minus what `omit` names | An empty `only` places no restriction, which is why a repository with no config is read whole. A pattern is read against the directory of **the config file that states it**. Anchoring follows the rules of `.gitignore`. | Pattern | Matches | | --- | --- | | `gen.go` | A file of that name at any depth | | `/gen.go`, `./gen.go` | The one beside this config file | | `gen/**` | That directory beside this config file, and no other | | `**/gen/**` | That directory at any depth | | `gen/` | That directory at any depth, the same as `**/gen/**` | | `/gen/`, `./gen/` | That directory beside this config file, the same as `gen/**` | | `*`, `?` | Within one path segment | A leading `./` anchors the same way as a leading `/`. A trailing `/` names a directory and everything in it. Without one, a pattern names a file, so `./vendor` matches only a file called `vendor`. Write `./vendor/` or `./vendor/**` for the directory. One report comes from the configuration rather than from the code. It fires when a file's `only` matches files, but an `only` above it removes them all, so the package is read as empty. ```console sub/a.go:1:1: filter.only stated in /repo/sub matches 1 file(s) here, but an only above it removes them all, so this package is read as empty ``` The report is that narrow on purpose. A package that reads nothing is usually the point, as with a root `only` naming one subtree, or an `omit` naming a directory. The cause is in the config files, so fix it there: change the nested `only`, or the `only` above it, so that the files are read. No directive silences this report, since nothing in the package is read. `filter` is still a valid rule name for `//declscope:ignore`, but such an ignore silences nothing, so the [`unused`](#unused-directives) rule reports it. ## Directives A **directive** is a line comment `//declscope:name`, with a lowercase name, no spaces, and any argument after a space. Any other comment starting with `declscope:` is [malformed](#malformed-directives). A trailing `// reason` is ignored. ```go //declscope:shared // used by the reporting code ``` | Directive | Level | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `//declscope:shared`, `//declscope:private` | Declaration or file | States the [scope](#scope-resolution). On a type it also reaches the type's [fields](#members), but not its methods | | `//declscope:ignore` | Declaration or file | Silences every rule the analyzer reports. [`overexported`](#silencing-it) must be named | | `//declscope:ignore ` | Declaration or file | Silences the named [rules](#rules), comma-separated. Naming [`filter`](#the-filter-rule) silences nothing | | `//declscope:core` | File | Joins the file to the [core namespace](#the-core-namespace) | | `//declscope:namespace ` | File | Joins the file to an [explicitly named namespace](#namespaces) | > [!CAUTION] > `//declscope:shared` was spelled `//declscope:package` before v0.19.0, and `defaults.unexported: shared` was `package`. v0.20.0 and later read neither. To upgrade from v0.18.x or earlier, go through v0.19.0 first and run `-fix` there: see [#186](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/issues/186). ### Placement A declaration-level directive goes in the doc comment, directly above the declaration. A file-level directive goes above the package clause. ```go //declscope:shared package database //declscope:shared func userSeed() {} ``` A directive on a block reaches every spec in it. A directive on one spec overrides the block's. ```go //declscope:shared var ( seed = 1 //declscope:private limit = 2 // this one is private ) ``` A directive on a type reaches its fields and its interface method names. It does not reach its methods, which take their own file's level.
Where a file-level directive may sit `//declscope:namespace` must come before the package clause. Three placements are accepted there.
PlacementExample
A blank line before package, as this README writes ```go //declscope:namespace billing package app ```
Directly above package ```go //declscope:namespace billing package app ```
At the bottom of the package doc comment, after a blank // line: Go's own convention for a directive in a doc comment ```go // Package app bills users. // //declscope:namespace billing package app ```
Go excludes a `//tool:name` comment from a doc comment, so none of them reaches the rendered documentation.
### Ignore levels - Every level is consulted. Keep your Go packages **flat** without letting them turn into a free-for-all. declscope holds each declaration to the file that declares it. Another file may not use it. This is the `private` that Go has no word for, checked at build time. ## Why Go has two levels of visibility, and the lower one covers the whole package. | Level | Reach | | --- | --- | | Exported | Every importer | | Unexported | **Every file in the package** | There is no third level. In a flat package, every helper is a package-wide name, and every field is a package-wide reach. Splitting the package to get a boundary has a price. - Import cycles, and interfaces written only to break them. - **Every name the two halves share has to be exported.** You wanted a boundary between two files, and you published an API. - **A wrong boundary costs more.** Moving a declaration between files is free. Moving it between packages breaks every importer. `internal/` does not help here. It limits who may import a package, but it adds no level below unexported. So most Go code is better off flat, and the cost appears inside the package. Teams handle this with a convention: *this helper belongs to this file.* The convention lives only in the heads of the people who wrote the package. An AI agent does not know it either. It sees an unexported helper in scope, so it calls it. It sees an unexported field, so it writes to it. Each edit compiles and passes a quick review, and the package becomes a mesh. declscope checks the convention instead. When an agent crosses a boundary, it is told what it crossed and given a fix. The decision is then written in the source, where the next agent reads it. ### What it reports One `database` package holds a repository per entity. ```go // user_repository.go package database import ( "context" "database/sql" "strings" "example.com/app/domain" ) type UserRepository struct{ db *sql.DB } func (r *UserRepository) Find(ctx context.Context, id int64) (*domain.User, error) { row := r.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = ?`, id) return scanUser(row) } func scanUser(row *sql.Row) (*domain.User, error) { var u domain.User var email string if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &email); err != nil { return nil, err } u.Email = normalizeEmail(email) return &u, nil } func normalizeEmail(s string) string { return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s)) } ``` ```go // order_repository.go package database import ( "database/sql" "example.com/app/domain" ) type OrderRepository struct{ db *sql.DB } func scanOrder(rows *sql.Rows) (domain.Order, error) { var o domain.Order var email string if err := rows.Scan(&o.ID, &email); err != nil { return domain.Order{}, err } o.BuyerEmail = normalizeEmail(email) return o, nil } ``` The two scan helpers are named apart by hand, since only one could be called `scan`. That mark says which repository owns which helper, and nothing holds anyone to it. `normalizeEmail` was written for `scanUser`. `scanOrder` calls it, and the compiler accepts that. ```console $ declscope ./... user_repository.go:28:6: func normalizeEmail is private to namespace "userRepository", but is used from namespace "orderRepository" order_repository.go:17:17: used here, in namespace "orderRepository" ``` A crossing has two answers. | Answer | How | | --- | --- | | Keep the boundary | Move the call inside the namespace | | Share on purpose | Write `//declscope:shared`, which `-fix` inserts | Here the helper belongs to neither repository. The repair is a third file, and a stated scope. ```go // email.go package database import "strings" //declscope:shared func normalizeEmail(s string) string { return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s)) } ``` > [!TIP] > `-fix` always widens, because that is the repair a tool can apply. It writes the directive where the declaration stands, and never moves a declaration to another file. Where the boundary is worth keeping, move the call yourself. ### Where declscope sits Three linters draw boundaries in Go, at three scales. ![A Go program drawn as nested frames. A directive that declscope cannot read belongs to the [`directive`](#malformed-directives) rule instead. #### Off, loose and strict | `rules.unused` | `//declscope:ignore` is reported when | `//declscope:shared` or `//declscope:private` is reported when | `-fix` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `off` | Never | Never | None | | `loose` | It silenced no report | Deleting it would change no declaration's scope under any config | None | | `strict` *(default)* | It silenced no report | Deleting it would change no declaration's scope under the current config | Deletes a redundant scope directive, unless [withheld](#the-strict-fix) | - One comment gets one report, however many declarations it reaches. A block's directive is reported once. - Without the directive, a declaration falls to the next row of [scope resolution](#scope-resolution). Only `defaults.unexported` there depends on the config. - Under `strict`, a directive that `loose` keeps also stays when deleting it would make a nearer directive redundant. - `off` still leaves the `directive` rule on. - An ignore of `boundary` is not reported where a file the build leaves out names a declaration it reaches, or for a field, its type: a literal written by position names only the type. That file may cross into it under another build tag, where the ignore silences the crossing. The run that reads the file still reports an ignore with nothing to silence. > [!WARNING] > Under `strict`, changing `defaults.unexported` changes the reports. With `unexported: shared`, every `//declscope:shared` on an unexported declaration that nothing else widens is reported, and one `-fix` run deletes them. `loose` never reports a directive only because it names the current default.
Example: one file under each mode ```go package app type user struct { //declscope:private name string } //declscope:shared func Helper() {} //declscope:ignore boundary func greet(u user) string { return u.name } ``` | Line | `off` | `loose` | `strict` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 4 | Nothing | Nothing | `unused //declscope:private on user.name: it already has private scope` | | 8 | Nothing | `unused //declscope:shared on Helper: nothing it reaches takes a scope` | `unused //declscope:shared on Helper: it already has shared scope` | | 11 | Nothing | `unused //declscope:ignore boundary on greet` | `unused //declscope:ignore boundary on greet` | Line 4 is where the modes differ. Deleting line 4 leaves `user.name` private only because `defaults.unexported` is private, which `loose` does not rely on.
#### Report messages Every unused report names the directive and says why it is unused. `loose` and `strict` word the reason differently. #### The strict fix `-fix` deletes a directive that `strict` reports, unless deleting it would change another report. Then the report stays, with no fix.
Example: one directive deleted, one withheld ```go // user.go package app //declscope:private func normalize() {} //declscope:private func trim() {} ``` ```go // order.go package app var _ = normalize ``` ```console $ declscope ./... # with rules.unused: strict user.go:4:6: func normalize is declared private by //declscope:private, but is used from namespace "order" order.go:3:9: used here, in namespace "order" user.go:3:1: unused //declscope:private on normalize: it already has private scope user.go:6:1: unused //declscope:private on trim: it already has private scope ``` `-fix` changes `user.go`. The `boundary` report names `normalize`'s directive, so that one stays. ```diff //declscope:private func normalize() {} -//declscope:private func trim() {} ```
#### Silencing an unused report | Ignore | Silences the unused report of | | --- | --- | | `//declscope:ignore unused` on a declaration | Every other directive on that declaration | | Bare `//declscope:ignore` on a declaration | The scope directive on that declaration. Not the other ignores there, so a group of ignores cannot excuse one another | | `//declscope:ignore unused`, or a bare one, above the package clause | Every other directive in the file | | Any ignore on a type or a block | Nothing inside it. For other rules it reaches inside, but here one ignore would hide every stale directive under it | **No ignore silences its own unused report.**

### Malformed directives Only `//declscope:name` is a directive. Any other comment starting with `declscope:`, and an unknown, conflicting or misplaced directive, is reported by the `directive` rule and has no effect.
Every malformed-directive report The rule is always on, and has no configuration key. `//declscope:ignore directive` silences it, on the declaration or above the package clause. `` stands for the directive's own name, such as `shared` or `core`. | Directive | Report | | --- | --- | | `//declscope:foo` on a declaration | `unknown directive declscope:foo` | | `//declscope:foo` above the package clause | `declscope:foo is not a file-level directive` | | `// declscope:shared`, `/*declscope:shared*/`, or any other comment starting with `declscope:` that is not `//declscope:name` | `malformed declscope directive: write it as //declscope:name` | | `//declscope:shared x`, or an argument to another directive that takes none | `//declscope: takes no argument` | | `//declscope:namespace` with no name | `declscope:namespace requires a name` | | `//declscope:namespace Billing` | `namespace "Billing" is not a valid lowerCamelCase identifier` | | `//declscope:private` and `//declscope:shared` together | `conflicting scope directives: ...` | | `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:namespace` together | `conflicting namespace directives: a core file's namespace is the core` | | `//declscope:ignore foo` | `unknown rule "foo" in declscope:ignore (want one of boundary, qualify, surplus, unused, directive, filter, overexported)` | | `//declscope:ignore ,` or `//declscope:ignore boundary,` | `empty rule name in declscope:ignore` | | The same directive twice on one declaration or file. ## Namespaces A **namespace** is the unit within which a `private` declaration may be used. By default each file is its own namespace, named after the file. | File | Namespace | | --- | --- | | `user_repository.go` | `userRepository` | | `user_repository_test.go` | `userRepository`. A test shares the namespace of its subject | | `parser_linux.go` | `parser`. A GOOS or GOARCH suffix is a build constraint, not a namespace | | `parser_test_linux.go` | `parserTest`. As in go/build, only a name ending in `_test.go` is a test | | `parser_linux.pb.go`, `parser.x_linux.go` | `parserPb`, `parserXLinux`. As in go/build, a suffix counts only before the first dot | | `user_id.go`, `user_ids.go`, `parse_json.go` | `userID`, `userIDs`, `parseJSON`. An initialism, or its plural, is spelled the way Go spells it | | `foo-bar.go`, `Foo.go` | `fooBar`, `foo`. Any separator, and a PascalCase stem, become lowerCamelCase | | `HTTPServer.go`, `URLs.go`, `IPv4.go` | `httpServer`, `urls`, `ipv4`. A leading initialism is lowered the way Go lowers one | | `2fa_auth.go`, `用户.go` | `2faAuth`, `用户`. Valid namespaces, but never a prefix: the first character must be a letter with a capital form | The namespace comes *from* the file name and is not equal to it. So you can rename a file without renaming what it declares. Files join an **explicitly named** namespace with a directive before the package clause. This is how one unit spans several files. The name must be an unexported identifier. ```go //declscope:namespace user package repo ``` ### The core namespace One namespace in a package may be its **core**: the unit the package is named for. Several files may carry `//declscope:core`, and they share the one core namespace. ```go // client.go //declscope:core package transport ``` The core has no prefix, so [the naming rule](#the-naming-rule) asks nothing of its declarations. No prefix still names exactly one unit. A test file joins the core when it tests a core file, as `client_test.go` tests `client.go`. The test file is matched by its whole name, so `client_linux_test.go` joins a core `client_linux.go` but not a core `client.go`. Only a test file joins: a core `client_test.go` does not take `client.go` into the core, and a core `client_linux.go` does not take `client.go`. A test file that names its own namespace with `//declscope:namespace` keeps it. > [!IMPORTANT] > `//declscope:core` sets the namespace and nothing else. It carries no scope. What it declares keeps the default scope | > | `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:shared` | Both apply. The file is core, and what it declares is package-wide | > | `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:namespace` | Refused. A core file's namespace *is* the core | ## Scopes The **subject** of the analysis is a package's unexported surface: its unexported package-level declarations, and the unexported [members](#members) of any type. An ignore counts as used whenever it covers a rule that would have fired, so overlapping ignores never make one another look unused. 452 - Ignores are consulted **before** the baseline. A suppression the baseline would also have absorbed still counts as used. 453 454 ### Unused directives 455 456 The `unused` rule reports a directive that changes nothing. A directive that declscope cannot read belongs to the [`directive`](#malformed-directives) rule instead. 457 458 #### Off, loose and strict 459 460 | `rules.unused` | `//declscope:ignore` is reported when | `//declscope:shared` or `//declscope:private` is reported when | `-fix` | 461 | --- | --- | --- | --- | 462 | `off` | Never | Never | None | 463 | `loose` | It silenced no report | Deleting it would change no declaration's scope under any config | None | 464 | `strict` *(default)* | It silenced no report | Deleting it would change no declaration's scope under the current config | Deletes a redundant scope directive, unless [withheld](#the-strict-fix) | 465 466 - One comment gets one report, however many declarations it reaches. A block's directive is reported once. 467 - Without the directive, a declaration falls to the next row of [scope resolution](#scope-resolution). Only `defaults.unexported` there depends on the config. 468 - Under `strict`, a directive that `loose` keeps also stays when deleting it would make a nearer directive redundant. 469 - `off` still leaves the `directive` rule on. 470 - An ignore of `boundary` is not reported where a file the build leaves out names a declaration it reaches, or for a field, its type: a literal written by position names only the type. That file may cross into it under another build tag, where the ignore silences the crossing. The run that reads the file still reports an ignore with nothing to silence. 471 472 > [!WARNING] 473 > Under `strict`, changing `defaults.unexported` changes the reports. With `unexported: shared`, every `//declscope:shared` on an unexported declaration that nothing else widens is reported, and one `-fix` run deletes them. `loose` never reports a directive only because it names the current default. 474 475

638 639 ## Namespaces 640 641 A **namespace** is the unit within which a `private` declaration may be used. By default each file is its own namespace, named after the file. 642 643 | File | Namespace | 644 | --- | --- | 645 | `user_repository.go` | `userRepository` | 646 | `user_repository_test.go` | `userRepository`. A test shares the namespace of its subject | 647 | `parser_linux.go` | `parser`. A GOOS or GOARCH suffix is a build constraint, not a namespace | 648 | `parser_test_linux.go` | `parserTest`. As in go/build, only a name ending in `_test.go` is a test | 649 | `parser_linux.pb.go`, `parser.x_linux.go` | `parserPb`, `parserXLinux`. As in go/build, a suffix counts only before the first dot | 650 | `user_id.go`, `user_ids.go`, `parse_json.go` | `userID`, `userIDs`, `parseJSON`. An initialism, or its plural, is spelled the way Go spells it | 651 | `foo-bar.go`, `Foo.go` | `fooBar`, `foo`. Any separator, and a PascalCase stem, become lowerCamelCase | 652 | `HTTPServer.go`, `URLs.go`, `IPv4.go` | `httpServer`, `urls`, `ipv4`. A leading initialism is lowered the way Go lowers one | 653 | `2fa_auth.go`, `用户.go` | `2faAuth`, `用户`. Valid namespaces, but never a prefix: the first character must be a letter with a capital form | 654 655 The namespace comes *from* the file name and is not equal to it. So you can rename a file without renaming what it declares. 656 657 Files join an **explicitly named** namespace with a directive before the package clause. This is how one unit spans several files. The name must be an unexported identifier. 658 659 ```go 660 //declscope:namespace user 661 package repo 662 ``` 663 664 ### The core namespace 665 666 One namespace in a package may be its **core**: the unit the package is named for. Several files may carry `//declscope:core`, and they share the one core namespace. 667 668 ```go 669 // client.go 670 //declscope:core 671 672 package transport 673 ``` 674 675 The core has no prefix, so [the naming rule](#the-naming-rule) asks nothing of its declarations. No prefix still names exactly one unit. 676 677 A test file joins the core when it tests a core file, as `client_test.go` tests `client.go`. The test file is matched by its whole name, so `client_linux_test.go` joins a core `client_linux.go` but not a core `client.go`. Only a test file joins: a core `client_test.go` does not take `client.go` into the core, and a core `client_linux.go` does not take `client.go`. A test file that names its own namespace with `//declscope:namespace` keeps it. 678 679 > [!IMPORTANT] 680 > `//declscope:core` sets the namespace and nothing else. It carries no scope. A core declaration still takes [`defaults.unexported`](#configuration): by default it is private *to the core*, and a file outside the core that names it crosses a boundary. 681 > 682 > | Written on a file | Effect | 683 > | --- | --- | 684 > | `//declscope:core` | The file joins the core. What it declares keeps the default scope | 685 > | `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:shared` | Both apply. The file is core, and what it declares is package-wide | 686 > | `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:namespace` | Refused. A core file's namespace *is* the core | 687 688 ## Scopes 689 690 The **subject** of the analysis is a package's unexported surface: its unexported package-level declarations, and the unexported [members](#members) of any type. 691 692 A **scope** is how far a declaration may be used. There are two. 693 694 | Scope | Meaning | Rust equivalent | 695 | --- | --- | --- | 696 | `shared` | Usable anywhere in the package | `pub(super)` | 697 | `private` | Usable only inside its own [namespace](#namespaces) | No modifier | 698 699 There is no `public`. Go already spells that with a capital letter, and declscope never sees a use beyond the package edge. 700 701 ### Scope resolution 702 703 A declaration's scope comes from the first row that applies. 704 705 | The declaration | Scope | 706 | --- | --- | 707 | Carries `//declscope:shared` or `//declscope:private` | The directive's | 708 | Is contained by something that carries one | The container's | 709 | Sits in a file carrying a [file-level directive](#directives) | The file's | 710 | Is exported | `shared` | 711 | Otherwise | [`defaults.unexported`](#configuration), which is `private` unless configured | 712 713 Containment means a [field](#members) inside its type, or a spec inside its `var`, `const` or `type` block. 714 715 An unexported declaration is `shared` only where something says so: a directive, or the `defaults` key. Its *name* plays no part. A prefix marks ownership and grants nothing. 716 717 > [!IMPORTANT] 718 > Exportedness decides the default, and nothing else. An **exported field of an unexported type** still resolves to `shared`, so making the type unexported protects nothing. 719 > 720 > State the boundary instead. `//declscope:private` on the type binds every field it reaches. 721 > 722 > ```go 723 > // Capitalized for encoding/json, not for an audience. 724 > //declscope:private 725 > type entry struct { 726 > Key string `json:"key"` 727 > Value []byte `json:"value"` 728 > } 729 > ``` 730 731 ### Members 732 733 A **member** is a name written *inside* a type's declaration: a struct's **field**, or an interface's **method name**. It is written inside its type, so its namespace is the type's file's, and the type's directive reaches it. 734 735 A **method with a receiver** is not a member. It is an ordinary top-level declaration, and its own file gives it its namespace. 736 737 | | Package-level declaration | Member | Method with a receiver | 738 | --- | --- | --- | --- | 739 | Bounding namespace | Its file's | Its **type**'s file's | Its file's | 740 | Contained by | Its `var`, `const` or `type` block | Its **type** | Nothing | 741 | [Naming rule](#the-naming-rule) | Applies | Does not apply | Only when filed away from its type | 742 743 The naming rule skips members because a member is never read on its own. Every use writes its value first, so `u.name` hands the reader `u` to follow. A method is read the same way, through its receiver. 744 745 What Go lacks for a member is encapsulation. Every unexported field is visible to the whole package. The `private` scope supplies it. 746 747
748 A type's methods filed in another file 749 750 Splitting a type's methods across files is ordinary Go. A builder often declares its state in one file and its chainable methods in another. 751 752 ```go 753 // statement.go (namespace: statement) 754 package database 755 756 type Statement struct { 757 Table string 758 wheres []string 759 } 760 ``` 761 ```go 762 // query.go (namespace: query) 763 package database 764 765 func (s *Statement) Where(cond string) *Statement { 766 s.wheres = append(s.wheres, cond) 767 return s 768 } 769 ``` 770 771 Writing `Where` in `query.go` is not itself a crossing. The field it reaches is one, and the report lands on `statement.go`. 772 773 ```console 774 $ declscope ./... 775 statement.go:5:2: field Statement.wheres is private to namespace "statement", but is used from namespace "query" 776 query.go:4:4: used here, in namespace "query" 777 query.go:4:22: used here, in namespace "query" 778 ``` 779 780 The naming rule asks the method to carry `query`. A method is read through its receiver, and `s.Where` points the reader at `Statement`'s unit, which does not hold it. 781 782 ```console 783 query.go:3:21: method Where does not carry namespace "query" anywhere in its name; rename it to QueryWhere, or to another name that carries "query" 784 ``` 785 786 Neither report asks for a rename here. The two files are one unit split in two, and `//declscope:namespace statement` on `query.go` settles both. 787 788

The violation is reported either way. A doubt withholds the fix, never the diagnostic. 1036 1037 > [!CAUTION] 1038 > Go resolves a name from the inside out, so a new name that is free at package level can still be bound at a use site. The wrong rename **compiles and computes something else**. 1039 > 1040 > ```go 1041 > var count = 10 1042 > func Add(fooCount int) int { return fooCount + count } // Add(1) == 11 1043 > ``` 1044 > ```go 1045 > // after a careless rename of count to fooCount 1046 > func Add(fooCount int) int { return fooCount + fooCount } // Add(1) == 2 1047 > ``` 1048 1049 A method, or a type that is embedded, is renamed only when the new name is free on every type that holds it. A method is also not renamed when an interface of the package asks for its old or new name, since a type assertion would change its answer. 1050 1051 A package that holds a non-Go source file, such as assembly (`.s`) for any architecture, gets no rename fix. Assembly names Go functions by text, which the rename cannot follow, and the build would fail at link time. Rename by hand, or add `//declscope:ignore qualify`. 1052 1053 ### `surplus` 1054 1055 `surplus` is the converse of `boundary`. It reports shared scope that no visible use from another namespace needs. 1056 1057 | `rules.surplus` | Reports | Fix | 1058 | --- | --- | --- | 1059 | `off` | Nothing | | 1060 | `loose` | A `//declscope:shared` that nothing it reaches needs | None | 1061 | `strict` *(default)* | What `loose` reports, plus each declaration a directive in use widens for nothing | Insert `//declscope:private` | 1062 1063 ```go 1064 // email.go 1065 package database 1066 1067 //declscope:shared 1068 func normalizeEmail(s string) string { return s } 1069 ``` 1070 1071 ```console 1072 $ declscope ./... 1073 email.go:3:1: //declscope:shared on normalizeEmail: no use from another namespace is visible to declscope 1074 ``` 1075 1076 One comment gets one report, however many declarations take their scope from it. A declaration that states its own scope does not depend on the comment, so it neither keeps it alive nor appears under it. 1077 1078 > [!IMPORTANT] 1079 > The rule concludes from an **absence**. A directive can hold up something declscope cannot see, so the rule stays quiet on any doubt. For the same reason `loose` offers no fix: its advice is to delete a directive. 1080 1081 #### `strict` 1082 1083 Under `loose`, one used declaration keeps its whole directive quiet. The rest of what the directive reaches may still be wider than it needs. `strict` reports each of those, and `-fix` narrows it. 1084 1085 ```go 1086 // account.go 1087 package bank 1088 1089 //declscope:shared 1090 type account struct { 1091 id int 1092 balance int 1093 } 1094 1095 func accountDeposit(a *account, n int) { a.balance += n } 1096 ``` 1097 1098 ```go 1099 // ledger.go 1100 package bank 1101 1102 func ledgerKey(a account) int { return a.id } 1103 ``` 1104 1105 ```console 1106 $ declscope ./... 1107 account.go:6:2: field account.balance takes shared scope from //declscope:shared on account, but no use from another namespace is visible to declscope 1108 ``` 1109 1110 `-fix` changes `account.go`: 1111 1112 ```diff 1113 //declscope:shared 1114 type account struct { 1115 - id int 1116 + id int 1117 + //declscope:private 1118 balance int 1119 } 1120 ``` 1121 1122 Every enclosing directive is judged the same way. 1123 1124 | The directive is on | Judged one by one | 1125 | --- | --- | 1126 | A struct or interface type | Each field, or each method name | 1127 | A `var`, `const` or `type` block | Each spec | 1128 | The file | Each declaration in the file, and each member of a type that states no scope | 1129 1130 `strict` is the default. `loose` checks only directives as a whole; select it explicitly if that is the policy your repository wants. 1131 1132 > [!TIP] 1133 > Convention puts private fields last, after the fields other namespaces read. The fix never reorders fields: order is observable through unkeyed composite literals, positional encodings, `unsafe` offsets and 64-bit atomic alignment. Move them yourself where none of those apply. 1134 1135 ## Unexporting what no importer uses 1136 1137 `declscope shrink` finds the exported declarations of `internal/` packages that nothing outside their package uses. With `-fix` it unexports them. 1138 1139 **Why it matters.** An exported declaration takes shared scope by default, so the analyzer never reports a boundary on it. An exported name that nothing outside needs hides a declaration from every check here. Unexported, it takes `private`, and the analyzer checks who reaches it. 1140 1141 **Why a subcommand.** The analyzer reads one package, and any importer might use an exported name. Inside `internal/`, Go limits the importers to one directory tree. `shrink` loads the whole module, so it sees every one of them. In a workspace, it loads every module of the workspace. A nested module whose path lies under an `internal/` parent can import the package too, so `shrink` loads it as well, and counts its uses. `go vet` and golangci-lint never run it. 1142 1143 ```go 1144 // internal/user/user.go 1145 package user 1146 1147 import "fmt" 1148 1149 func Load(id int) string { return Format(id) } 1150 1151 // Format renders an ID for display. 1152 func Format(id int) string { return fmt.Sprint(id) } 1153 1154 type Record struct { 1155 ID int 1156 Name string 1157 } 1158 1159 func Dump(r Record) { fmt.Println(r) } 1160 ``` 1161 1162 `api/api.go` calls `user.Load` and names `user.Dump`. Nothing outside `user` names `Format` or `Record`: 1163 1164 ```console 1165 $ declscope shrink 1166 internal/user/user.go:8:6: func Format is exported, but nothing outside example.com/app/internal/user uses it 1167 ``` 1168 1169 `declscope shrink -fix` renames `Format` to `format`, and the doc comment that opens with it. `Record` is not reported: `fmt.Println` reads its fields through reflection, which is a use. 1170 1171 ### Run it before the analyzer 1172 1173 **Apply `shrink -fix` first, then work on the analyzer's reports.** A declaration it unexports becomes private to its namespace. Wherever another file uses it, the analyzer now reports a crossing, which `declscope -fix` or a move settles. The other order takes a second round. 1174 1175 ```console 1176 $ declscope shrink -fix ./... 1177 $ declscope ./... 1178 ``` 1179 1180 Run them in the same order in CI. `shrink` exits 3 when it reports anything, as the analyzer does. With `-fix`, only the reports left without a fix count. 1181 1182 ### Patterns 1183 1184 The patterns only choose which packages are reported. To find uses, `shrink` always reads every package of the module, whatever the patterns name. 1185 1186 For example, this reports only on `internal/user`: 1187 1188 ```console 1189 $ declscope shrink ./internal/user/... 1190 internal/user/user.go:8:6: func Format is exported, but nothing outside example.com/app/internal/user uses it 1191 ``` 1192 1193 `Load` is not reported, although `api/` is outside the pattern. `api/api.go` calls `user.Load`, and that call is a use. 1194 1195 Otherwise, a pattern behaves as it does for `go vet`. 1196 1197
1198 What counts as a use, and when the fix is withheld 1199 1200 A fix is offered only where no use can exist outside the package. Where a use may exist but cannot be proved, the report stays and says why no fix is offered. 1201 1202 1203 1204 1205 1206 1207 1208 1223 1224 1225 1226 1239 1240 1241 1242 1252 1253 1254 1255 1263 1264 1265 1266 1284 1285 1286 1287 1297 1298 1299 1300 1308 1309 1310 1311 1321 1322 1323 1324 1332 1333 1334 1335 1345 1346 1347 1348

declscope

\n\n [![CI](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/actions/workflows/ci.yml)\n [![Codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/mpyw/declscope/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/mpyw/declscope)\n [![Go Reference](https://pkg.go.dev/badge/github.com/mpyw/declscope.svg)](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/mpyw/declscope)\n\n \n

\n \n\n

Write-ups: 🇯🇵 JP · 🇺🇸 EN

\n
\n\nKeep your Go packages **flat** without letting them turn into a free-for-all.\n\ndeclscope holds each declaration to the file that declares it. Another file may not use it. This is the `private` that Go has no word for, checked at build time.\n\n## Why\n\nGo has two levels of visibility, and the lower one covers the whole package.\n\n| Level | Reach |\n| --- | --- |\n| Exported | Every importer |\n| Unexported | **Every file in the package** |\n\nThere is no third level. In a flat package, every helper is a package-wide name, and every field is a package-wide reach.\n\nSplitting the package to get a boundary has a price.\n\n- Import cycles, and interfaces written only to break them.\n- **Every name the two halves share has to be exported.** You wanted a boundary between two files, and you published an API.\n- **A wrong boundary costs more.** Moving a declaration between files is free. Moving it between packages breaks every importer.\n\n`internal/` does not help here. It limits who may import a package, but it adds no level below unexported. So most Go code is better off flat, and the cost appears inside the package.\n\nTeams handle this with a convention: *this helper belongs to this file.* The convention lives only in the heads of the people who wrote the package.\n\nAn AI agent does not know it either. It sees an unexported helper in scope, so it calls it. It sees an unexported field, so it writes to it. Each edit compiles and passes a quick review, and the package becomes a mesh.\n\ndeclscope checks the convention instead. When an agent crosses a boundary, it is told what it crossed and given a fix. The decision is then written in the source, where the next agent reads it.\n\n### What it reports\n\nOne `database` package holds a repository per entity.\n\n```go\n// user_repository.go\npackage database\n\nimport (\n\t\"context\"\n\t\"database/sql\"\n\t\"strings\"\n\n\t\"example.com/app/domain\"\n)\n\ntype UserRepository struct{ db *sql.DB }\n\nfunc (r *UserRepository) Find(ctx context.Context, id int64) (*domain.User, error) {\n\trow := r.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = ?`, id)\n\treturn scanUser(row)\n}\n\nfunc scanUser(row *sql.Row) (*domain.User, error) {\n\tvar u domain.User\n\tvar email string\n\tif err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &email); err != nil {\n\t\treturn nil, err\n\t}\n\tu.Email = normalizeEmail(email)\n\treturn &u, nil\n}\n\nfunc normalizeEmail(s string) string {\n\treturn strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s))\n}\n```\n```go\n// order_repository.go\npackage database\n\nimport (\n\t\"database/sql\"\n\n\t\"example.com/app/domain\"\n)\n\ntype OrderRepository struct{ db *sql.DB }\n\nfunc scanOrder(rows *sql.Rows) (domain.Order, error) {\n\tvar o domain.Order\n\tvar email string\n\tif err := rows.Scan(&o.ID, &email); err != nil {\n\t\treturn domain.Order{}, err\n\t}\n\to.BuyerEmail = normalizeEmail(email)\n\treturn o, nil\n}\n```\n\nThe two scan helpers are named apart by hand, since only one could be called `scan`. That mark says which repository owns which helper, and nothing holds anyone to it.\n\n`normalizeEmail` was written for `scanUser`. `scanOrder` calls it, and the compiler accepts that.\n\n```console\n$ declscope ./...\nuser_repository.go:28:6: func normalizeEmail is private to namespace \"userRepository\", but is used from namespace \"orderRepository\"\norder_repository.go:17:17: \tused here, in namespace \"orderRepository\"\n```\n\nA crossing has two answers.\n\n| Answer | How |\n| --- | --- |\n| Keep the boundary | Move the call inside the namespace |\n| Share on purpose | Write `//declscope:shared`, which `-fix` inserts |\n\nHere the helper belongs to neither repository. The repair is a third file, and a stated scope.\n\n```go\n// email.go\npackage database\n\nimport \"strings\"\n\n//declscope:shared\nfunc normalizeEmail(s string) string {\n\treturn strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s))\n}\n```\n\n> [!TIP]\n> `-fix` always widens, because that is the repair a tool can apply. It writes the directive where the declaration stands, and never moves a declaration to another file. Where the boundary is worth keeping, move the call yourself.\n\n### Where declscope sits\n\nThree linters draw boundaries in Go, at three scales.\n\n![A Go program drawn as nested frames. Between the api and database packages, depguard asks whether one package may import another. A green arrow runs from api to database, and a red one back from database to api is crossed out. Inside database, between user_repository.go and order_repository.go, declscope asks whether one file may reach another's declaration. A red arrow from scanOrder to normalizeEmail is crossed out. At the edge of the program, deadcode asks whether anything is reachable at all. The mail package sits greyed out with no arrow entering it, captioned unreachable.](docs/boundaries.png)\n\n| Linter | Scale | The question it answers |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| [`depguard`](https://github.com/OpenPeeDeeP/depguard) | Between packages | May this package import that one? |\n| **declscope** | Within one package | May this file reach that declaration? |\n| [`deadcode`](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode) | Whole program | Is this reachable at all? |\n\nThe three compose. `depguard` keeps the package graph honest, declscope keeps each package honest inside, and `deadcode` removes what neither needs to reach.\n\n## Install\n\n| Method | Command | Needs |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| **[mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/)** *(recommended)* | `mise use \"github:mpyw/declscope@0.24.1\"` | Nothing. Installs the prebuilt binary |\n| `go tool` | `go get -tool github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest` | Go 1.27+ |\n| `go install` | `go install github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest` | Go 1.27+ |\n| Release archive | See below | Nothing |\n\n```bash\ndeclscope ./...\n```\n\n
\nPin a version, run through go vet, or install from an archive\n\n`mise use` pins the version in the project's `mise.toml`, so every checkout and CI run the same one. Add `-g` to install it for every project on your machine instead.\n\n```toml\n[tools]\n\"github:mpyw/declscope\" = \"0.24.1\"\n```\n\nAs a tool dependency in `go.mod`:\n\n```bash\ngo get -tool github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest\ngo tool declscope ./...\n```\n\nThrough `go vet`, which runs it with the same package loading as the rest of your vet checks:\n\n```bash\ngo vet -vettool=$(which declscope) ./...\n```\n\n> [!WARNING]\n> **`go vet` does not see changes to config or baseline files.** It caches the result of each package, and the cache key does not include these files. After a change to either one, run `go vet` once with **`-a`**:\n>\n> ```bash\n> go vet -a -vettool=$(which declscope) ./...\n> ```\n>\n> Without `-a`, `go vet` can report the result of the old configuration. New diagnostics can be missing, and old ones can remain. Running `declscope` directly is not affected.\n\nWithout installing anything:\n\n```bash\ngo run github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest ./...\n```\n\nFrom a release archive, verified against the published checksums:\n\n```bash\nVERSION=0.24.1\ncurl -LO \"https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/releases/download/v${VERSION}/declscope_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz\"\ncurl -LO \"https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt\"\nshasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing\ntar xzf \"declscope_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz\"\n```\n\n
\n\n### Flags\n\n| Flag | Default | Effect |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `-config` | *(discovered)* | Path to a YAML config file. Skips the [`.declscope.yaml` lookup](#configuration) |\n| `-test` | `true` | Analyze `*_test.go` files as well |\n| `-fix` | `false` | Apply suggested fixes |\n| `-diff` | `false` | With `-fix`, print a diff instead of writing files |\n| `-V=full` | | Print the version and exit. `go run`, or a build with `-buildvcs=false`, answers `devel` |\n\n`-test`, `-fix` and `-diff` come from `go/analysis`. `declscope -help` lists the rest.\n\n### Subcommands\n\n| Command | What it does | Flags of its own |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `declscope survey [packages]` | [Report what was checked and what it found](#measuring-what-is-there), one row per package | `-format`, `-test`, `-config`, `-allow-errors` |\n| `declscope inspect ` | [Report the shape of one package](#measuring-what-is-there): its namespaces and the crossings between them | `-format`, `-test`, `-config` |\n| `declscope baseline [packages]` | [Record the violations a codebase already has](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase), `shrink`'s included | `-config`, `-o`, `-shrink`, `-merge` |\n| `declscope shrink [packages]` | [Unexport what no importer uses](#unexporting-what-no-importer-uses), inside `internal/` | `-fix`, `-config` |\n| `declscope skill install` | Install the authoring and adoption skills for an AI agent | `--agent`, `--scope` |\n\n`declscope -help` lists each one's flags.\n\n## Configuration\n\nEvery setting is optional. The table below lists each setting and its default value. The YAML block shows all available keys; some values are examples.\n\n```yaml\ndefaults:\n unexported: private # shared | private\n\nrules:\n naming:\n qualify: never # always | never | ondemand\n exported: false # true | false\n vocabulary:\n mouse: [wheel]\n boundary: on # off | on\n surplus: strict # off | loose | strict\n unused: strict # off | loose | strict\n\nfilter:\n only: [] # nothing outside these, when set\n omit:\n - \"**/mock_*.go\" # and not these\n\nbaseline: .declscope-baseline.yaml\n```\n\n| Key | Values | Default | Effect |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| `defaults.unexported` | `shared`, `private` | `private` | Scope of a declaration that carries no directive and inherits none |\n| `rules.naming.qualify` | `always`, `never`, `ondemand` | `never` | When a name must carry its namespace. See [the naming rule](#when-it-applies) |\n| `rules.naming.exported` | `true`, `false` | `false` | Whether the naming rule also reaches exported declarations. The rename is never offered there |\n| `rules.naming.vocabulary` | Namespace to a list of words | None | Extra words that carry a namespace. See [what carries a namespace](#what-carries-a-namespace) |\n| `rules.boundary` | `off`, `on` | `on` | Whether the [`boundary`](#boundary) rule reports. See [reach without a boundary](#reach-without-a-boundary) |\n| `rules.surplus` | `off`, `loose`, `strict` | `strict` | How much the [`surplus`](#surplus) rule reports. See [strict](#strict) |\n| `rules.unused` | `off`, `loose`, `strict` | `strict` | How much the [`unused`](#unused-directives) rule reports. See [off, loose and strict](#off-loose-and-strict) |\n| `filter.only` | Path globs | None | When set, no file outside them is read. Empty places no restriction |\n| `filter.omit` | Path globs | None | Files taken back out, whether or not `only` let them through |\n| `baseline` | A path relative to the config file | The nearest `.declscope-baseline.yaml` | The [baseline](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase) to consult |\n\n> [!TIP]\n> For the recommended checks, put this in `.declscope.yaml`:\n>\n> ```yaml\n> rules:\n> naming:\n> qualify: ondemand\n> exported: true\n> ```\n>\n> `ondemand` checks names once a package has a second namespace. `exported: true` includes exported declarations. `surplus` and `unused` default to `strict`.\n\n- The file is `.declscope.yaml` or `.declscope.yml`. An empty one changes nothing.\n- [`-config`](#flags) names one file, and reads no other.\n- An **unknown key is an error**, and so is a value a key does not accept. The message names what the section does take, so a typo never leaves a rule at its default in silence.\n\n`defaults` takes only `unexported`, because an exported declaration has no scope to default.\n\n### How two config files compose\n\nEvery `.declscope.yaml` between the analyzed package and the module root is read, **outermost first**. A nearer file does not replace the one above it. Each key composes on its own.\n\n| Key | Down the chain |\n| --- | --- |\n| `defaults.*`, `rules.*` except `vocabulary`, `baseline` | The nearest file that states the key wins. A key no file states takes the built-in default |\n| `rules.naming.vocabulary` | Merged per namespace. The nearer file wins the namespaces it states |\n| `filter.only` | **Intersected.** A file is read when it matches every stating file's list |\n| `filter.omit` | **Unioned.** A file matching any level's list is not read |\n\n> [!IMPORTANT]\n> **A config file can only ever shrink what is read.** An `omit` written at the root holds everywhere below it, and no nested file can undo it. `filter` has no negation, so nothing like `.gitignore`'s `!` can put a path back.\n\n### The filter rule\n\n`filter` decides which files are read at all. A file matches a list when it matches **any** pattern in it.\n\n| Written | Read |\n| --- | --- |\n| Neither | Every file |\n| `only` alone | Nothing outside the patterns |\n| `omit` alone | Everything except the patterns |\n| Both | What `only` admits, minus what `omit` names |\n\nAn empty `only` places no restriction, which is why a repository with no config is read whole.\n\nA pattern is read against the directory of **the config file that states it**. Anchoring follows the rules of `.gitignore`.\n\n| Pattern | Matches |\n| --- | --- |\n| `gen.go` | A file of that name at any depth |\n| `/gen.go`, `./gen.go` | The one beside this config file |\n| `gen/**` | That directory beside this config file, and no other |\n| `**/gen/**` | That directory at any depth |\n| `gen/` | That directory at any depth, the same as `**/gen/**` |\n| `/gen/`, `./gen/` | That directory beside this config file, the same as `gen/**` |\n| `*`, `?` | Within one path segment |\n\nA leading `./` anchors the same way as a leading `/`. A trailing `/` names a directory and everything in it. Without one, a pattern names a file, so `./vendor` matches only a file called `vendor`. Write `./vendor/` or `./vendor/**` for the directory.\n\nOne report comes from the configuration rather than from the code. It fires when a file's `only` matches files, but an `only` above it removes them all, so the package is read as empty.\n\n```console\nsub/a.go:1:1: filter.only stated in /repo/sub matches 1 file(s) here, but an only above it removes them all, so this package is read as empty\n```\n\nThe report is that narrow on purpose. A package that reads nothing is usually the point, as with a root `only` naming one subtree, or an `omit` naming a directory.\n\nThe cause is in the config files, so fix it there: change the nested `only`, or the `only` above it, so that the files are read. No directive silences this report, since nothing in the package is read. `filter` is still a valid rule name for `//declscope:ignore`, but such an ignore silences nothing, so the [`unused`](#unused-directives) rule reports it.\n\n## Directives\n\nA **directive** is a line comment `//declscope:name`, with a lowercase name, no spaces, and any argument after a space. Any other comment starting with `declscope:` is [malformed](#malformed-directives). A trailing `// reason` is ignored.\n\n```go\n//declscope:shared // used by the reporting code\n```\n\n| Directive | Level | Effect |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `//declscope:shared`, `//declscope:private` | Declaration or file | States the [scope](#scope-resolution). On a type it also reaches the type's [fields](#members), but not its methods |\n| `//declscope:ignore` | Declaration or file | Silences every rule the analyzer reports. [`overexported`](#silencing-it) must be named |\n| `//declscope:ignore ` | Declaration or file | Silences the named [rules](#rules), comma-separated. A file-level directive goes above the package clause.\n\n```go\n//declscope:shared\n\npackage database\n\n//declscope:shared\nfunc userSeed() {}\n```\n\nA directive on a block reaches every spec in it.
